lesson.title: Squeezing the South: Winfield Scott's Anaconda Plan
lesson.summary: Early in the war, aging General Winfield Scott proposed a strategy of naval blockade and control of the Mississippi River meant to slowly strangle the Confederacy's economy rather than seek a quick decisive battle, a plan mocked at the time but largely followed over the following four years.
lesson.body:
In the spring of 1861, with the Confederacy freshly formed after the fall of Fort Sumter, the Union's senior military commander faced a strategic question with no obvious answer: how do you defeat a rebellion spread across a landmass roughly the size of Western Europe without simply marching an army straight at its capital and hoping for the best. General Winfield Scott, who at seventy four years old had commanded American armies since the War of 1812 and had led the victorious campaign into Mexico City in 1847, argued against the popular Northern demand for a quick strike on Richmond. Instead he proposed a slower, more methodical approach built on two main pillars.

The first pillar was a naval blockade of the entire Confederate coastline, from Virginia around Florida and along the Gulf of Mexico to Texas, meant to cut the South off from selling its cotton abroad and from importing the weapons, manufactured goods, and supplies its underdeveloped industrial base could not produce on its own. The second pillar called for Union control of the Mississippi River, achieved by capturing key points along its length, which would split the Confederacy in two, cutting Texas, Arkansas, and most of Louisiana off from the rest of the rebellion and denying Confederate armies the river's use for moving troops and supplies. Scott believed this combination would gradually squeeze the Confederate economy and war effort until Southern resistance simply collapsed, with far less bloodshed than a series of head-on battles.

Newspapers and much of the Northern public mocked the plan almost as soon as it became known, nicknaming it the Anaconda Plan after the South American snake that kills by constriction, and arguing that it was too slow and too passive for a war many Northerners expected to end within months. Scott himself retired from active command in November 1861, in part because of his age and health, and the early war effort instead focused on the more direct campaigns that public opinion demanded, including the disastrous Union defeat at the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861, which quickly deflated hopes for a short war.

Even so, the core logic of Scott's plan proved durable. The Union blockade expanded steadily throughout the war and, while never fully airtight, choked off enough Confederate trade to badly damage the Southern economy over time. Union campaigns along the Mississippi, culminating in the capture of Vicksburg in July 1863, eventually achieved exactly the kind of Confederacy-splitting control Scott had envisioned. In hindsight, much of the Union's actual winning strategy, patient, resource-driven, and aimed at the Confederacy's economic capacity rather than a single decisive battle, ended up resembling the plan that had been ridiculed as too cautious in the war's opening months.
